```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| output: false
import {selectControl, loadWeekData, issueTargets, mmeSkillByLead, mmeSkillMaps, mmePatterns, mmeForecastMaps, mmeScoresByLead, mmeFlexible} from "../assets/leads/leads.js"
mme = loadWeekData("../assets/monthly-mme-2023/")
geo = ({indonesia: await FileAttachment("../data/boundaries/indonesia.geojson").json(),
  provinces: await FileAttachment("../data/boundaries/provinces.geojson").json(),
  neighbours: await FileAttachment("../data/boundaries/neighbours.geojson").json()})
leadChoices = mme.targets.map(t => [String(t.lead), `Lead ${t.lead}: ${t.label}`])
modelChoices = mme.models.map(m => [m, m === "MME" ? "MME (the ensemble)" : m])
memberChoices = modelChoices.filter(([m]) => m !== "MME")
```

::: {.eyebrow}
Monthly · Multi-model ensemble · Full Indonesia
:::

The [seasonal ensemble](seasonal-mme-2023.qmd) calibrated seven models started on
1 June 2023 for six overlapping three-month seasons. This case keeps the start, the
models, the training years and the settings, and changes one thing: the target is a
**single month**, July to December 2023. It shows the same outputs: skill for every
member and for the ensemble (MME), EOF patterns and CCA modes, calibrated forecasts,
and the flexible forecast.

Everything is at CHIRPS v3.0's native 0.05° grid: the 69,640 pixels that touch
Indonesia's 38-province boundary and have data in every training month. All numbers
on this page come from the [executed notebook](../notebooks/monthly-mme-2023.ipynb). Hover,
tap or use the arrow keys on any map or chart to read values; maps load when you
choose them, and the maps in a group zoom and pan together.

::: {.callout-note title="The short result"}
- **A single month is harder than a season.** The ensemble's cross-validated
  correlation is 0.32, 0.33, 0.39 and 0.50 for July to October, then
  0.17 and 0.06 for November and December. The three-month seasons that
  start in those months scored 0.55, 0.62 and 0.58 for the first three;
  only October matches its season (0.50 against 0.50 for
  October-December).
- **The best month is four months ahead.** October scores highest, above the nearer
  months: skill follows the target month, not the lead.
- **The ensemble beats CFSv2 alone in four months of six.** It is above CFSv2 for
  July, September, October and November and has the higher correlation in
  74% to 90% of pixels there. For August and December it is slightly below.
- **It is never the best member.** By correlation the ensemble ranks third of eight
  for July to September, second for October, and fifth for November and December.
- **Calibration costs more here than for seasons.** The plain average of the raw
  models correlates at 0.50, 0.50 and 0.53 for July to September, well above
  the calibrated ensemble. Only for October is the calibrated ensemble higher
  (0.50 against 0.48).
- **Probabilities still beat climatology at every lead**, by less than for seasons:
  the ensemble's cross-validated RPSS is 0.13 to 0.25 for July to October and
  0.08 and 0.05 after that.
- **In 2023 the ensemble was dry in every month.** That was wrong for July, when
  51% of the area ended near normal and the hit rate was 22%, and right from
  September to December, when 47% to 78% of the area ended below normal.
:::

## Why 1 June, and what that does not establish

The date is the seasonal ensemble's, so the two pages can be read side by side. It
was chosen there from a [scan of every start month and lead](seasonal-mme-2023.qmd#why-1-june)
for **three-month seasons**. No such scan was made for single months. This page
therefore does not claim that 1 June is the best start for monthly targets; it
measures what the same start gives.

## Which models, and why these

The same eleven catalog models were candidates. Before any skill was computed, a
script downloaded each one with PyCPT's own `download_data` for every target month
and recorded whether the download worked, every training year held data, the 2023
forecast held data, and the **returned target month was the one requested**.

| Model | Jul | Aug | Sep | Oct | Nov | Dec | In the ensemble |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CFSv2 | ok | ok | ok | ok | ok | ok | all six leads |
| GEOSS2S | ok | ok | ok | ok | ok | ok | all six leads |
| CanSIPSIC3 | ok | ok | ok | ok | ok | ok | all six leads |
| CCSM4 | ok | ok | ok | ok | ok | ok | all six leads |
| CESM1 | ok | ok | ok | ok | ok | ok | all six leads |
| SPEAR | ok | ok | ok | ok | ok | ok | all six leads |
| SEAS51c | ok | ok | ok | ok | ok | November returned | leads 1 to 5 |
| GCFS2p1 | 1992, 2020 missing | same | same | same | same | November returned | no |
| SPSv3p5 | 5 years missing | same | same | same | same | November returned | no |
| METEOFRANCE9 | 1992 missing, no 2023 forecast | same | same | same | same | November returned | no |
| CanSIPSIC4 | no 2023 forecast | same | same | same | same | same | no |

: Availability of single-month targets for a 1 June 2023 issue with training target years 1992-2020, measured on 16 November 2026. Source: [availability.json](../data/monthly-mme-2023/availability.json), written by `research/scripts/check_lead_mme_availability.py`.

Two points shaped the design:

- **Training uses target years 1992-2020 (29 years) for every model**, the years of
  the seasonal ensemble, so all members and both pages share one sample.
- **SEAS51c forecasts six months**, so from 1 June it ends in November. It joins
  July to November only. The ensemble has **seven members at leads 1 to 5 and six
  at lead 6**. The seasonal ensemble lost SEAS51c after lead 3, because a
  three-month season needs the model to reach its last month.

::: {.callout-warning title="A month beyond a model's range did not fail"}
For three-month targets, asking for a season beyond a model's range fails with an
error. For single months it did not. Asking PyCPT for December from a 1 June start
returned a file without an error for SEAS51c, GCFS2p1, SPSv3p5 and METEOFRANCE9;
in each case the file's own dates were **November's**, the last month those models
reach. The table marks these "November returned". The fit script compares the
returned target dates with the request for every model and lead before fitting, so
none of them entered the December ensemble.
:::

::: {.story-interactive}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof timelineLead = selectControl("Highlight", leadChoices, "1")
issueTargets(mme, timelineLead)
```
:::

## One calibration, 82 times

Each model is calibrated at each lead with **CCA** (3 predictor and 3 predictand
EOFs, 2 CCA modes) and **PCR** (3 predictor EOFs), cross-validation window 5, the
settings of the seasonal ensemble. Each fit is one call of PyCPT's
`evaluate_models`: 82 fits in all. At 0.05° a fit took 15 to 37 minutes (median 33)
with many running side by side.

The observations are CHIRPS v3.0 monthly totals built from dekads. A pixel is kept
if any part of it touches a province of the supplied 38-province boundary, so
coastal pixels and small islands are included, and if it has data in all 29
training years of every target month: 69,640 pixels.

The ensemble is PyCPT's `construct_mme`: the **equal-weight average** of the
members' calibrated forecasts, taken separately for the deterministic forecast, the
prediction error variance and the three category probabilities. The notebook
confirms it: the ensemble forecast equals the mean of its members exactly, and
CPT's Pearson map equals the correlation recomputed from the cross-validated
hindcasts to within 0.0001.

## Skill of every member, and of the ensemble

Area-weighted means over Indonesia, cross-validated over 1992-2020. **Pearson
correlation** is 0 for no linear relationship. **2AFC** is the chance that the
hindcasts rank two different years in the observed order, 50% for no skill
[(Mason and Weigel 2009)](https://doi.org/10.1175/2008MWR2553.1).

::: {.story-interactive}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof chartMethod = selectControl("Calibration", ["CCA", "PCR"], "CCA")
viewof chartMetric = selectControl("Score", [["Pearson", "Pearson correlation"], ["2AFC (%)", "2AFC"], ["CV RPSS", "Cross-validated RPSS"]], "Pearson")
mmeSkillByLead(mme, chartMethod, chartMetric)
```
:::

| Lead | Target | Members | MME | CFSv2 alone | Best member | Raw multi-model mean | Pixels where MME beats CFSv2 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Jul 2023 | 7 | 0.32 | 0.21 | SPEAR, 0.36 | 0.50 | 90% |
| 2 | Aug 2023 | 7 | 0.33 | 0.35 | GEOSS2S, 0.40 | 0.50 | 38% |
| 3 | Sep 2023 | 7 | 0.39 | 0.33 | GEOSS2S, 0.43 | 0.53 | 87% |
| 4 | Oct 2023 | 7 | 0.50 | 0.45 | GEOSS2S, 0.52 | 0.48 | 75% |
| 5 | Nov 2023 | 7 | 0.17 | 0.12 | SEAS51c, 0.26 | 0.26 | 74% |
| 6 | Dec 2023 | 6 | 0.06 | 0.08 | CFSv2, 0.08 | 0.16 | 44% |

: Pearson correlation of the CCA calibrations, area-weighted mean over 69,640 pixels, cross-validated 1992-2020. Source: [mme-against-members.csv](../data/monthly-mme-2023/mme-against-members.csv).

Read across a row. The ensemble is above CFSv2 for July, September, October and
November, and slightly below it for August and December. It is never first: third
of eight for July to September, second of eight for October behind GEOSS2S, fifth of
eight for November and fifth of seven for December. No member is best throughout
either: SPEAR leads for July, GEOSS2S for August to October, SEAS51c for November.
With PCR the ensemble is almost the same
(0.31, 0.31, 0.38, 0.51, 0.15, 0.07).

The raw column matters more here than on the seasonal page. Averaging the models'
**raw** rainfall, with no calibration, correlates with the observations at
0.50, 0.50 and 0.53 for July to September, against 0.32, 0.33 and 0.39
for the calibrated ensemble. It is also higher for November and December
(0.26 and 0.16 against 0.17 and 0.06). Only for October does calibration
come out ahead. Two things should be kept in mind. The raw correlations involve no
fitting, so they do not carry the downward bias of cross-validation described
below. And the raw average is not a forecast product: it has model biases and no
probabilities. This page does not establish why three EOFs keep less of the
models' signal for a month than for a season.

### Probabilities, cross-validated

PyCPT's own probabilistic scores are computed from in-sample probabilities; its
source code calls them "unrealistically optimistic". The notebook builds
cross-validated tercile probabilities instead. For each training year it leaves out
that year and its two neighbours on each side, takes the tercile boundaries and the
error spread from the remaining years, and centres a Student's t distribution on
the left-out year's cross-validated hindcast. The ranked probability skill score
(**RPSS**) compares those probabilities with a climatological forecast built the
same way; above 0 means the model adds information. This construction is this
tutorial's, not CPT's.

| Lead | Target | MME | CFSv2 alone | Highest member |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Jul 2023 | 0.13 | 0.06 | SPEAR, 0.14 |
| 2 | Aug 2023 | 0.14 | 0.15 | GEOSS2S, 0.18 |
| 3 | Sep 2023 | 0.17 | 0.13 | GEOSS2S, 0.16 |
| 4 | Oct 2023 | 0.25 | 0.21 | GEOSS2S, 0.27 |
| 5 | Nov 2023 | 0.08 | 0.04 | SEAS51c, 0.09 |
| 6 | Dec 2023 | 0.05 | 0.04 | SPEAR, 0.04 |

: Cross-validated RPSS of the CCA calibrations against a climatological forecast put through the same steps, area-weighted mean, 1992-2020. Source: [skill-by-lead.csv](../data/monthly-mme-2023/skill-by-lead.csv).

By this score the ensemble does better than by correlation: first for September and
December, second for July, October and November, third for August. Its
probabilities are positive against climatology at every lead, 0.13 to 0.25 for July
to October and 0.08 and 0.05 for November and December. The seasonal ensemble
scored 0.23 to 0.32 for its first four seasons.

### Why a correlation near zero is not "no skill" here

Cross-validation biases correlation downward. A forecast with **no model at all**,
the mean of the other years, correlates *negatively* with the observations: leaving
a wet year out lowers the mean of the rest. The notebook measures it: the no-model
forecast has an area-mean correlation of -0.24 to -0.41 at these six leads
[(Barnston and van den Dool 1993)](https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0442(1993)006%3C0963:ADICVS%3E2.0.CO;2).

So 0 is not the no-skill level of a cross-validated correlation, and the 0.06 for
December is not as close to "nothing" as it looks. A calibrated model's correlation
is not simply shifted by that amount either, which is why this page compares
correlations with each other, and reads them alongside the RPSS, whose reference is
that same no-model forecast.

### Where the skill is

::: {.story-interactive}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof mapModel = selectControl("Model", modelChoices, "MME")
viewof mapMethod = selectControl("Calibration", [["CCA", "CCA"], ["PCR", "PCR"], ["raw", "None (raw model)"]], "CCA")
viewof mapMetric = selectControl("Score", [["pearson", "Pearson correlation"], ["rpss", "Cross-validated RPSS"]], "pearson")
mmeSkillMaps(mme, geo, mapModel, mapMethod, mapMetric)
```
:::

## EOF patterns and CCA modes

CCA does not relate the two fields pixel by pixel. It first reduces each to a few
**EOFs**, patterns that explain the most year-to-year variance, each with a score
per year. It then finds pairs of combinations of those, the **CCA modes**, whose
score series are as correlated as possible. These views show what each calibration
is built from.

Choose a model, a lead and a mode. The top map is the pattern in the model's
rainfall over the predictor box, the second the pattern in observed rainfall over
Indonesia, and the chart their scores in each training year.

::: {.story-interactive}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof patModel = selectControl("Model", memberChoices, "CFSv2")
viewof patLead = selectControl("Lead", leadChoices, "1")
viewof patKind = selectControl("Show", [["cca", "CCA mode"], ["eof", "EOF"]], "cca")
viewof patMode = selectControl("Mode", [["1", "1"], ["2", "2"], ["3", "3 (EOF only)"]], "1")
mmePatterns(mme, geo, patLead, patModel, patKind, patMode)
```
:::

How to read them, and how not to:

- The patterns come from the fit to **all 29 training years**, not from the
  cross-validation folds. A canonical correlation of 0.69 to 0.91 for the first
  July mode describes how well the fitted pair matches in-sample. The
  cross-validated correlation of the forecasts it produces is 0.17 to 0.36.
- The predictand EOFs depend on the observations alone, so they are identical for
  every model at a given lead (the notebook checks this). For July the first three
  explain 40.0%, 10.7% and 9.3% of the variance, 60% together; for
  July-September the seasonal ensemble's three explained 73%. A single month has
  more variance that three patterns do not describe.
- Loadings are in CPT's units and are scaled here so each map's largest absolute
  value is 1. Sign and shape carry meaning; magnitude does not.

## The forecasts, model by model

Each calibrated member gives a deterministic total and three tercile probabilities
at every pixel; the ensemble averages them. The first view is PyCPT's standard
probabilistic map: the colour is the most likely category, darker where its
probability is higher. Others show the total, and the anomaly against the
1992-2020 mean of the same month.

::: {.story-interactive}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof fcModel = selectControl("Model", modelChoices, "MME")
viewof fcMethod = selectControl("Calibration", ["CCA", "PCR"], "CCA")
viewof fcView = selectControl("Show", [["probability", "Most likely category and probability"], ["anomaly", "Forecast anomaly (mm)"], ["percent", "Forecast as % of normal"], ["total", "Forecast total"], ["observedCategory", "Observed category"], ["observedAnomaly", "Observed anomaly (mm)"], ["observed", "Observed total"]], "probability")
mmeForecastMaps(mme, geo, fcModel, fcMethod, fcView)
```
:::

### Against what happened

Each lead's target is checked against the observed total. The **hit rate** is the
share of area where the most likely category was the one observed; the grey
squares show what always forecasting the most widespread category would have
scored, a reference chosen with hindsight.

::: {.story-interactive}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof scoreMethod = selectControl("Calibration", ["CCA", "PCR"], "CCA")
viewof scoreMetric = selectControl("Score", [["hit", "Hit rate"], ["rpss", "RPSS"], ["rmse", "RMSE"]], "hit")
mmeScoresByLead(mme, scoreMethod, scoreMetric)
```
:::

| Lead | Target | Observed below / near / above (% of area) | MME forecast below / above (% of area) | MME hit rate | Reference hit rate | MME RPSS |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Jul 2023 | 13 / 51 / 36 | 72 / 19 | 22% | 51% (near) | -0.18 |
| 2 | Aug 2023 | 27 / 47 / 26 | 68 / 16 | 44% | 47% (near) | 0.07 |
| 3 | Sep 2023 | 47 / 39 / 14 | 91 / 3 | 48% | 47% (below) | 0.18 |
| 4 | Oct 2023 | 78 / 19 / 3 | 95 / 3 | 79% | 78% (below) | 0.44 |
| 5 | Nov 2023 | 61 / 29 / 9 | 91 / 6 | 61% | 61% (below) | 0.26 |
| 6 | Dec 2023 | 50 / 32 / 18 | 68 / 27 | 55% | 50% (below) | 0.18 |

: The CCA ensemble against each target's observation, area-weighted over 69,640 pixels. RPSS here is against 33/34/33% odds, for one outcome per lead. Sources: [issued-2023-06-forecasts.csv](../data/monthly-mme-2023/issued-2023-06-forecasts.csv), [issued-2023-06-observed.csv](../data/monthly-mme-2023/issued-2023-06-observed.csv).

The ensemble put most of Indonesia in the dry category in every month. For July
that was wrong: 51% of the area ended near normal and only 13% below, the hit rate
was 22% against a reference of 51%, and the RPSS was negative (-0.18), worse
than climatological odds. August was mixed and the ensemble fell 2.5 points short of
the reference. From September the dry signal was what happened: 47% to 78% of
the area ended below normal, the hit rate matched or beat the hindsight reference,
and the RPSS was 0.18 to 0.44, highest for October.

One member shows what averaging guards against. For October, GEOSS2S
had the highest cross-validated correlation of all (0.52), yet in 2023 its most
likely category was right over only 11% of the area, while every other member
scored 74% to 79%. The ensemble, which contains it, scored 79%. One
outcome per lead describes 2023; it is not a measure of skill.

## The flexible forecast: probability of exceedance

A tercile map answers one question. The **flexible forecast** answers others: the
probability that the month's total exceeds a chosen amount at each pixel. PyCPT's
`construct_flex_fcst` builds it from the ensemble's deterministic forecast and its
prediction error variance, as a Student's t distribution
([chapter 5](../learn/05-probabilistic-forecasts.ipynb) compares its conventions
with CPT's native ones).

The default threshold is each pixel's **climatological median**, so the map reads
as "chance of a wetter than median month" and 50% means no information. Choose
another percentile to ask about dry or wet extremes. **Click any pixel** to draw
its curves: the forecast distribution against the climatology, as probability of
exceedance and as density, with the observed total marked.

::: {.story-interactive}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof flexLead = selectControl("Lead", leadChoices, "1")
viewof flexPercentile = selectControl("Threshold", [["10", "10th percentile (very dry)"], ["20", "20th percentile"], ["33", "33rd percentile"], ["50", "Median"], ["67", "67th percentile"], ["80", "80th percentile"], ["90", "90th percentile (very wet)"]], "50")
mmeFlexible(mme, geo, flexLead, flexPercentile)
```
:::

| Lead | Target | Mean chance of exceeding the median | Area with chance above 50% | Area observed above the median |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Jul 2023 | 43% | 25% | 62% |
| 2 | Aug 2023 | 43% | 23% | 46% |
| 3 | Sep 2023 | 35% | 8% | 28% |
| 4 | Oct 2023 | 32% | 4% | 8% |
| 5 | Nov 2023 | 36% | 9% | 20% |
| 6 | Dec 2023 | 43% | 30% | 32% |

: The CCA ensemble's flexible forecast, area-weighted. Source: [flexible-forecast.csv](../data/monthly-mme-2023/flexible-forecast.csv).

The table tells the July story again: the forecast gave only 25% of the area a
better than even chance of a wetter than median month, and 62% of the area ended
above its median. For October the two numbers are 4% and 8%.

The curves in the browser are computed from four stored fields per lead (forecast
centre and scale, climatological mean and scale) with the same formula as PyCPT.
The notebook confirms that those fields reproduce PyCPT's own exceedance
probabilities exactly (largest difference 0.0 percentage points). The fitted
climatology is a normal distribution, as in PyCPT's own flexible-forecast figure;
the green dots are the percentiles of the 29 observed totals, which show where
that normal curve fits the data and where it does not.

Like the tercile probabilities, these assume the t distribution describes the
forecast error well. The cross-validated RPSS above is this page's only test of
that. Where a pixel's forecast curve is as wide as its climatology curve, or wider,
the forecast is saying little more than climatology there.

## What this case shows, and what it does not

This is one issue date, seven models, one set of fixed settings and one verifying
year per target. It shows that from a 1 June start a calibrated multi-model
ensemble has usable skill for the single months July to October, less than for the
seasons that contain them, and little for November and December. It shows the
ensemble above CFSv2 alone in four months of six and never the best member, and a
raw multi-model average that correlates better than the calibrated ensemble in five
months of six.

It does not show that 1 June is the best start for monthly targets, since no scan
of start months was made for single months. It does not show how other settings
behave: the settings (3 EOFs, 2 CCA modes) were those of the seasonal ensemble,
fixed before any skill was computed and not tuned per model or for monthly targets.

::: {.callout-tip title="Read it with the seasonal ensemble"}
The [seasonal ensemble](seasonal-mme-2023.qmd) uses the same models, start, training
years and settings for three-month totals. The
[single-model monthly page](monthly-leads-2023.qmd), issued 1 November 2023, asks
the monthly question of CFSv2 alone for December to May. The subseasonal ensembles
([dekad](dekad-mme-2023.qmd), [weekly](week-mme-2023.qmd), [pentad](pentad-mme-2023.qmd))
show the same outputs for five subseasonal models.
:::
